The option row is the one that repays a second look. One contract covers a hundred ETF shares, so it carries about $50,000 of exposure, while a one-month at-the-money contract on an underlying moving 16 per cent a year costs roughly $920 to buy — the standard approximation for an at-the-money option is 0.4 × price × volatility × √time, which is 0.4 × $500 × 0.16 × √(1÷12) = $9.24 a share. The exposure is more than fifty times the outlay, and the outlay is also the entire loss. No other row has those two properties at once, and that combination is why options are simultaneously the most and the least dangerous object in the table, depending only on which side of the contract you took.
